ABOUT_HEAD: A B.Tech physics project about one question and an honest answer.
ALSO: Whether EWMA or GARCH forecasts of next month's volatility beat simply assuming it looks like last month, tested walk-forward over 60 stocks and ten years.
ANN_TEXT: Our ANN (a standard artificial neural network) learns to read the ten settings from prices purely from examples. It produced the settings behind the 210-stock studies on this site.
A_LONG: Real option prices bend: protection against a fall usually costs more than a bet on a rise. Double Heston bends the same way, and on all 2,400 real NSE option surfaces we tested, its best fit beat one fixed volatility.
BACKTEST: With the settings our ANN reads from each day's own quotes, Double Heston priced that day's options better than a same-day Black–Scholes fit on 4.8% of 12,265 stock-days (589 of them). Carried to the next day, its settings beat Black–Scholes carried forward on 19.1%.
BEND: Black–Scholes prices every strike at the same volatility, so its smile is flat. Double Heston's two moving volatilities, tied to the price by a negative ρ, make protection against falls dearer: the line bends.
BEND_HEAD: One fixed volatility draws a flat line. Real prices bend.

EQ_CALL: C = e^(−rT) [ F·P₁ − K·P₂ ],   Pⱼ = ½ + (1/π) ∫₀^∞ Re[ e^(−iu·ln(K/F)) φⱼ(u) / (iu) ] du
EQ_PRICE: dS = (r − q) S dt + √v₁ S dW₁ + √v₂ S dW₂
EQ_VAR: dvᵢ = κᵢ (θᵢ − vᵢ) dt + ξᵢ √vᵢ dZᵢ,   corr(dWᵢ, dZᵢ) = ρᵢ,   i = 1, 2

f-price: Think of a boat on a river. The current carries it steadily downstream: that's the drift, r − q. Two kinds of waves rock it at once, short choppy ones and long swells. How rough each kind is right now is v₁ and v₂.
So the price wanders at random, and how wildly depends on two separate, changing levels of jumpiness.
f-variance: Picture a ball on a spring. θ is where the spring rests, κ is how stiff it is, and ξ is how hard someone keeps shaking it. ρ says which way the shaking leans.
In stock markets fear rises when prices fall, so ρ is usually negative, and that is what makes protection against a fall cost more.
f-cf: Two independent dice. To find the chance of each total you could list all 36 combinations, or combine each die's fingerprint with one multiplication. Independence is what makes the shortcut work.
That is why two factors cost little more to price than one.
f-call: Like a receipt for a bet. One line is what you expect to collect if the share ends above the strike (F·P₁). The next is the strike you expect to pay (K·P₂). The difference, brought back to today's money, is the fair price.
The integral is only the step that turns the model's fingerprint into those two chances.
f-mc: Instead of working out a die's average on paper, roll it 20,000 times and average the rolls.
If the formula and the simulation agree, the formula is coded right. They agree to within the simulation's own margin of error.
f-feller: A ball on a spring above the floor. If the spring pulls back hard enough (2κθ) compared with how hard it's shaken (ξ²), the ball never touches the floor.
Here the floor is zero variance. At the starting settings both factors break the condition, so the simulator stops the variance at zero instead of letting it go negative.
s-v₀: It sets the price of options that expire soon, before the weather has time to change.
s-θ: The climate: what the weather averages out to.
It matters most for options with a long time to run.
s-κ: How quickly the sky clears after a storm.
Option prices barely depend on it, which is why equally good fits disagree about it most.
s-ξ: How changeable the weather is: calm and predictable, or sun and hail in the same hour.
More of it makes extreme moves likelier, so options far from today's price get dearer.
s-ρ: Whether storms tend to arrive when prices drop.
In stock markets they usually do, so ρ is usually negative.
bend: Black–Scholes draws the market with a ruler: one straight volatility for every strike. Double Heston uses a flexible curve.
Real option prices bend, so the curve fits and the ruler can't.
decay: Two cups of coffee cooling: a small cup is cold in minutes, a big pot stays warm for hours. Same law, different speeds.
Half of a shock to the fast factor is gone in 51 days; in the slow factor it takes 1.4 years.
factors: Two dogs walked side by side, one on a short leash and one on a long one. The first darts about but stays close; the second wanders slowly and far.
The fast factor jitters and snaps back; the slow one drifts.
skew: A fresh scare matters a lot for next week and much less for next year, because it has time to fade.
So the extra cost of protection against a fall shrinks as expiry gets further away.
fan: Like a weather forecast cone: tomorrow is fairly certain, next month much less.
The shaded bands show how far simulated prices spread over a year. Averaging what an option pays across paths like these gives the Monte Carlo price.
surface: A relief map. Across is the strike, down is time to expiry, and colour is the height: implied volatility.
One look shows the smile at every expiry at once, steepest for short-dated options.
proof1: Like copying a song perfectly by ear, yet naming the wrong instruments.
The optimizer reproduced the prices almost exactly, but the settings it found scored 1.80, where 1.00 is always guessing the typical value.
proof2: Different magnets can raise the same ferrofluid surface.
On 99% of real surfaces, more than one set of settings priced the options equally well, and those sets were 3.9 times as far apart as two random guesses.
hist: Many witnesses describe the same car. If they agreed, every bar would sit near zero.
Bars far to the right are surfaces whose equally good fits disagreed a lot.
params: Some things every thermometer agrees on, like the room's temperature. Others you can't read off the room at all, like how fast it would cool if the heating went off.
Today's level (v₀) is pinned down by prices; the speeds back to normal (κ) are not.
magnets: Two people can draw the same smile with different pens.
Bharti Airtel's 39-day options were fitted equally well by two very different sets of ten settings.
part: Two maps that match street for street in the town centre but disagree about the countryside nobody visits.
Where options trade, the two fits agree. Beyond them, where no price can check them, they part.
six: Six different recipes that bake the same cake.
Where the spikes bunch, the prices pin that setting down; where they scatter, they don't.
stock: A scale that weighs you correctly every morning but reports a different height each day.
The price error stays small day after day while the distance between equally good fits stays large.
heldout: A student who did well on the practice papers but slipped in the real exam.
On 8 later dates the ANN's prices were off by 17.4%, against 4.3% for the best possible fit.
backtest: A new gadget that beats the old ruler about one day in twenty.
With the ANN's settings, Double Heston priced better than a same-day Black–Scholes fit on 4.8% of stock-days.
pinn: A student who also has to obey the textbook, not just copy past answers.
On real NIFTY options the physics-informed calibrator was off by 2.48 volatility points, against 2.98 for Black–Scholes, and was the best model on 4 of 10 days.

FORMULAS: The price moves with two variances
dS = (r − q) S dt + √v₁ S dW₁ + √v₂ S dW₂
Over a tiny moment of time, the share price drifts at the interest rate minus the dividend yield, and gets two random kicks. How big each kick is depends on one of the two variances.
the two variances, slow and fast
Each variance drifts back to normal
dvᵢ = κᵢ (θᵢ − vᵢ) dt + ξᵢ √vᵢ dZᵢ,   corr(dWᵢ, dZᵢ) = ρᵢ,   i = 1, 2

Each variance is pulled back toward its long-run level θ at speed κ, and shaken by random shocks of size ξ. Its shocks move with the price's shocks at correlation ρ. A negative ρ means falls come with rising volatility, which is what tilts the smile.
the long-run level it returns to
the link between price and variance shocks
1 for the slow factor, 2 for the fast one

The characteristic function φ is a compact fingerprint of where the price could end up. Because the two factors are independent, the model's fingerprint is just the product of each factor's own, so pricing stays fast.
the model's fingerprint, read at frequency u
the slow and fast factors' own fingerprints
C = e^(−rT) [ F·P₁ − K·P₂ ],   Pⱼ = ½ + (1/π) ∫₀^∞ Re[ e^(−iu·ln(K/F)) φⱼ(u) / (iu) ] du

A call is worth what you expect to receive above the strike, minus what you expect to pay, brought back to today's money. P₂ is the chance, under the pricing measure, that the option ends in the money; P₁ is the same chance counted in shares. Both come out of the fingerprint through one integral (Gil-Pelaez). The code uses the “little trap” form (Albrecher et al., 2007), which avoids a branch-cut error in the 1993 formula at long expiries.
real part of a complex number

Monte Carlo prices the same option the slow way: simulate 20,000 possible paths of the price and both variances, average what the call pays at expiry, and discount. The paths use full-truncation Euler steps and antithetic pairs. For the NIFTY 23,150 call it gives ₹597.10 ± 3.56, against ₹600.40 from the formula: inside the simulation's own margin of error.
the share price at expiry on path n
what a call pays at expiry
When a factor can't touch zero

If 2κθ is bigger than ξ², that factor's variance never reaches zero. Real markets often break this. When a simulated variance would go below zero, the simulator holds it at zero for that step (full truncation), so prices stay valid.
the speed, long-run level and shake of factor i

LIMITS: No jumps: the largest one-day moves are still underestimated.
Dividends are supported but set to zero; one interest rate for every maturity.
Prices are frictionless. Real trading crosses a bid–ask spread.
End-of-day research data has closing prices only, no bid–ask quotes.
A typical surface has 17 of the 20 target option slots quoted (between 10 and 20 on 80% of surfaces).
MARKET_SUB: Official NSE closing prices, 1 Jul 2026 to 25 Sep 2026, 62 trading days. Live prices from Upstox are planned for the same places; this version shows the closes.
MATHS_INTRO: An option's price depends on how jumpy the stock will be before it expires. Black–Scholes assumes one fixed jumpiness. Double Heston (Christoffersen, Heston and Jacobs, 2009) lets it move, and splits it into two parts that move on their own: a fast one for sudden scares and a slow one for long moods. Below is the whole model, one formula at a time.
MATHS_STEPS: The stock's variance is v₁ + v₂. Each factor pulls back toward its long-run level θ at speed κ, is shaken by ξ, and moves with the price at correlation ρ. A negative ρ means falls come with rising volatility: that tilts the smile.
Because the two factors are independent, the model's characteristic function is the product of each factor's own. That's what keeps pricing fast.

The option price comes from inverting the characteristic function (Gil-Pelaez). The code uses the 'little trap' form (Albrecher et al., 2007), which avoids a branch-cut error in the 1993 formula at long maturities.
Monte Carlo prices the same option by simulating 20,000 paths with full-truncation Euler steps and antithetic pairs. The two methods agree within the simulation's standard error.
If 2κθ > ξ², a factor's variance never reaches zero. Real markets often break it; full truncation keeps the simulation valid when it does.
METHOD: Prices come from the characteristic-function formula and are checked against Monte Carlo simulation.
Research data: official NSE end-of-day files. Every dataset, its size and what it was used for is listed on the Results page.
Every real-market result was re-run after three pipeline bugs were found and fixed, and checked against a flat volatility, which a true best fit can never lose to.
MODEL_EXPLAIN: The starting settings assume 20% volatility. On 25 Sep 2026 the market was pricing about 11.4%, so the model charges more. Lower today's level (v₀) and the gap closes. There's no fit button: the Results page explains why a computer can't pick all ten settings for you.
MODEL_SOURCE: Option prices: NSE closing prices, 25 Sep 2026. Forward from NIFTY October futures (23,263.60). Rate: RBI 91-day T-bill, 15 Jul observation carried forward, as in the research.

PA_HEAD: What the physics buys: a PINN against an ANN
PA_LEDE: Two identical networks saw the same 48 exact Double Heston prices. The ANN learned from those prices alone. The PINN also had to obey the model's pricing equation at 4,096 points and the option's payoff at expiry. Below, both price surfaces at today's volatility, drawn in 3D against the exact pricer.

ANN error on the same points
smaller pricing-equation error for the PINN
PA_REPLAY: Replay the training and the difference grows. The ANN's impossible prices fell to 93 by step 800, then climbed back to 187 as it fitted its 48 prices ever more tightly. The PINN's fell to zero: the equation kept it honest where it had no data.
PA_RESULT: On 2,000 fresh points the PINN's error was 0.8% of the average price, against 5.7% for the ANN, and it broke the pricing equation 35 times less. Where it had no data, the ANN guessed: on the slice above it priced 187 of 1,271 points below zero by more than 0.2% of the strike, which no option can be worth. The PINN priced none.
PER_PARAM: Split by setting, the pattern is physical. Today's level (v₀) is pinned down: equally good fits agree on it more closely than random sets would. The speeds back to normal (κ) are not pinned down at all; the best fit's speed sat at the edge of the allowed range on 45% (slow) and 73% (fast) of surfaces.
PINN_MARKET: On real NIFTY options (10 high-volatility days in April 2026, 1,750 held-out quotes) our physics-informed calibrator priced with a median error of 2.48 volatility points, against 2.98 for Black–Scholes and 2.52 for a classical Double Heston fit, in 1.2 s instead of 25 s. It was the best model on 4 of the 10 days.
PINN_TEXT: Our PINNs (physics-informed neural networks) are also trained on the model's own pricing equation, so their answers must obey the physics, not just match examples. The Double Heston PINN learned from exact prices plus the pricing equation at 18,000 points, and reproduces the exact pricer to 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ (about 0.1 volatility points) on 8,192 points it never saw. On 40 controlled test surfaces it beat a refitted one-factor Heston, which beat Black–Scholes, every time.
PROOF1: We generated 60 option surfaces from known settings and asked a classical optimizer to find them again, from 4 starting points each. It matched the prices almost exactly: a median price error of 9.16 × 10⁻⁸. The settings it found scored 1.80 on recovery, where 1.00 is what you'd get by always guessing the typical value, and lower is better.
PROOF1_HEAD: Simulated surfaces, where the right answer is known
PROOF1_NET: Our neural network (a standard ANN, which learns only from examples) reads the settings from prices and scores 0.80 on the RMSE-based version of the same score, where the optimizer scores 3.00. It does better by leaning toward typical values; the one setting it reads well is today's level (v₀, 0.47).
PROOF2: On 2,400 real surfaces (40 of NSE's most traded stocks over 60 days) we started the fit from 16 places each time. On 99% of them, more than one set of settings priced the options equally well, within 10% of the best fit's price error. Those equally good fits sat a median 4.64 apart, against 1.18 for two settings picked at random from the training data: 3.9 times as far.

Double Heston against one flat volatilit: A tailored suit against one size fits all.
On a typical surface the best Double Heston fit had 23% less price error, and it was ahead on all 2,400.
Fitting simulated prices: Tracing a drawing so closely you can't see the original underneath.
The optimizer's prices matched the simulated ones almost exactly.
Reading the settings back: Copying a song perfectly by ear, yet naming the wrong instruments.
1.80 means the recovered settings were further off than always guessing the typical value (1.00).
Several equally good fits: 99% of real surfaces had more than one equally good set of settings.
How far apart they sat: Two maps that agree on every street but put the landmarks in very different places.
Equally good fits sat 3.9 times as far apart as two random sets of settings.
Today's level: The room temperature: every thermometer agrees on it.
Equally good fits agreed on today's level more closely than random settings would.
Speeds back to normal: Judging how fast a spring snaps back from one photo of it at rest.
Prices barely depend on the speed, so equally good fits put it almost anywhere.
ANN, reading the settings: A student who learned from worked examples and plays safe by answering near the average.
0.80 beats always guessing (1.00) and the optimizer (3.00), mostly by reading today's level well.
ANN on dates it never saw: Good on the practice papers, worse in the real exam.
On new dates its prices were off by 17.4%, about four times the best possible fit.
ANN settings against Black–Scholes: A new gadget that beats the old ruler about one day in twenty.
Reading the settings from prices didn't make Double Heston better than the simplest model most of the time.
Next day, against Black–Scholes: Yesterday's forecast, judged on today's weather.
Settings carried to the next day beat Black–Scholes carried forward about one day in five.
PINN fidelity: A student who also has to obey the textbook.
Its prices match the exact formula to about 0.1 volatility points.
PINN, controlled test: Three runners, forty races, the same finishing order every time.
The PINN beat a refitted one-factor Heston on every surface, and Heston beat Black–Scholes.
PINN calibrator on NIFTY: Measured like a thermometer's error, in volatility points.
2.48 points against 2.98 for Black–Scholes, on quotes it never saw.
PINN against ANN (demonstration): Two students, the same lessons; one also had to obey the textbook.
The one that obeyed the pricing equation was about seven times more accurate and priced nothing impossible.

SETTINGS: How jumpy the stock is right now. Variance is volatility squared: 0.02 is about 14% a year.
Options cost more now, short-dated ones most.
The level the jumpiness settles back to over time.
How fast jumpiness returns to its long-run level after a shock. Half of a shock is gone after ln 2 ÷ κ years: 1.4 years for the slow factor, 51 days for the fast one.
Shocks fade faster, so the factor matters less for long-dated options.
How much the jumpiness itself jumps around.
The smile curves more: options far from today's price cost more.
Whether jumpiness rises when the price falls (negative) or when it rises (positive), from −1 to 1.
Toward −1: protection against falls gets dearer than bets on rises, so the smile tilts more.
